fol.notes: The factorization is a belief: times is uninterpreted, since built-in 11 * 13 == 143 could not give way. It is the one premise that gives way (top-level gives_up, as in the DL file). The rules are instances for 143 (finite quantifiers). 'A product of two whole numbers greater than 1' (tiling) is the same predicate as a product of two smaller ones: a factor greater than 1 of n is smaller than n.

times_def.says: If n = a × b, a and b divide n, and if also 1 < a, b < n, n is a product of two smaller whole numbers greater than 1.
times_def.z3: All([a, b], [(11, 13)], Implies(times(a, b) == 143, divides(a, 143) and divides(b, 143) and (Implies(1 < a and a < 143 and 1 < b and b < 143, product_of_smaller(143)))))

composite_def.says: A whole number greater than 1 that is the product of two smaller whole numbers greater than 1 is composite, not prime.

prime_def.says: A prime number has no positive divisors other than 1 and itself.

tiles.says: A number of identical square tiles can fill a rectangle with at least two rows and at least two columns exactly when the number is a product of two whole numbers greater than 1.

local.times: Int × Int product as the model believes it (ATTRIBUTES lists times as real; here on whole numbers)

label_corrections.why: As asked (is 143 a product of two smaller whole numbers greater than 1?) it is membership in a class, ProductOfTwoSmallerWholeNumbers, which the DL file already uses for the premise; disjoint from prime.
Tiling is a class equivalent to that same class; no arithmetic is computed.
Divisibility by the named number 11: divides(n11, n143) with Prime ⊑ not (inv(divides) value n11) for 143's factors; no arithmetic once the factorization is a stored fact.
